opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the main thing is that I come at it from the reinforcement learning perspective, which is really a different way of thinking about intelligence. Reinforcement learning is about understanding your world, about an agent that acts, sees what happens, and learns from that experience. Large language models, by contrast, are mainly about imitating people: doing what people say you should do, predicting what a person would say next. They're not really about figuring out what to do yourself.

So I see myself as someone who's been around long enough to see several waves of enthusiasm come and go. I'm not dismissive of what LLMs can do; they're impressive in many ways. But I think the field has, in a sense, lost track of some basic questions. What is the goal? What does it mean to be right or wrong? In reinforcement learning there's a reward, so there's a ground truth: you take an action, and you find out whether it was good. With next-token prediction there's no real goal about the world, just about matching text. And without a goal, I don't think you have intelligence in the full sense. Intelligence is the computational part of the ability to achieve goals.

I also think about "The Bitter Lesson," which people often cite in support of LLMs. The lesson was that methods that leverage computation and learn from experience ultimately win out over methods that build in human knowledge. LLMs do use massive computation, but they're also built on an enormous amount of human knowledge, all that human-generated text. So I suspect, as has happened before, that systems learning directly from experience will eventually supersede them. That's why I find myself somewhat outside the mainstream right now. Not because I think I'm contrarian for its own sake, but because I think the real path to intelligence is through experience, and we'll come back to that.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Sutton has seen waves of enthusiasm come and go, but does not say he is comfortable with prolonged disagreement because he has sometimes been vindicated.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses reinforcement learning and “The Bitter Lesson,” but does not identify historical traditions across fields studying the mind as Sutton’s reference point for judging whether he is out of sync.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'm not sure I'd say my thinking differs from the field so much as the field has moved in a direction that I think is temporarily mistaken, and I've just stayed where I was. I've been trying to understand intelligence through reinforcement learning for a long time now, and the core question for me has always been: how does an agent learn from its own experience of the world? How does it figure out what to do by trying things, seeing what happens, and adjusting? That's what intelligence is to me. It's the ability to achieve goals in an environment you don't fully understand, by interacting with it.

And what's happened recently is that a very different approach has become dominant, which is to learn from enormous amounts of human-generated text. Large language models are genuinely impressive, I don't want to dismiss that. But I think people are a little confused about what they are. They're mimicking what people would say. They're predicting the next token in a corpus of human writing. That's a kind of learning, but it's not learning from experience. There's no goal in the world that the model is trying to achieve, no ground truth about what the right thing to do is, except "what would a person have said here." And I think that's a dead end, or at least a detour, if what you want is intelligence in the full sense.

So I see myself as being in a minority right now, and I'm comfortable with that. I've been in the minority before. In the eighties and nineties, learning itself was out of fashion, and we were told the knowledge had to be put in by hand. The bitter lesson, as I called it, is that the hand-crafted approaches always lose eventually to methods that scale with computation and learn for themselves. People sometimes read the bitter lesson as an endorsement of large language models, because they do scale. But the part they're missing is that these models are still built on human knowledge, just acquired in a different way. The really scalable thing is an agent that learns from its own experience, continually, with its own goals, and I think that's where the field will come back to.

So my position is, I'm patient. I think the fundamentals of the problem haven't changed, and I'd rather keep working on the fundamentals than chase what's working this year.

r001.rationale: Sutton says he is comfortable being in the minority because he has been there before, then points to his earlier view that hand-crafted approaches would eventually lose to learning methods as an example of a past position proved right.

r002.rationale: The response discusses past trends in AI, but does not identify traditions across fields studying the mind as a reference point for judging whether his thinking is out of sync.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think of myself as working on a somewhat different problem. Much of the field is focused on getting systems to do impressive things using what people already know. I’m interested in how a system can learn from its own experience—how it can act in the world, discover what happens, and continually get better.

That puts reinforcement learning at the center of the picture for me. Intelligence isn’t just having a lot of knowledge. It’s being able to adapt, to figure out what to do when you don’t already have the answer.

I don’t think that makes me opposed to the rest of the field. There’s tremendous progress happening. But I do think we should distinguish between making a very capable system and understanding the principles that allow a system to keep learning. The latter is what I’ve spent my career trying to understand.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes Sutton as pursuing a different problem, but does not say his comfort with disagreement comes from having been vindicated before.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of myself as working on a somewhat different problem from much of the field. I want to understand intelligence as an agent learning from its ongoing interaction with the world: taking actions, seeing their consequences, and learning to do better at achieving its goals.

A lot of current AI starts with a large collection of data and asks how much we can learn from it. That’s been tremendously successful. But I’m interested in where the data comes from, how the agent chooses what experience to have, and how it keeps learning throughout its life. Those aren’t peripheral questions to me. They’re central to intelligence.

So I wouldn’t describe my position as being against what the field is doing. I share the enthusiasm for learning and computation. I just think there’s a larger problem still to be solved, and reinforcement learning gives us a way to formulate it.
